title: Beef, steak, ribeye, lean and fat portions

content.title: About
content.content: Ribeye steak is a cut taken from the rib section of a beef carcass. It combines lean muscle fibers with a marbled fat core, giving it a juicy, flavorful character. The steak can be grilled, pan‑seared, or oven‑roasted, and it is also enjoyed raw as steak tartare.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “ribeye” comes from the eye‑shaped fat marbling visible in the meat.
Marbling improves tenderness and flavor, making ribeye one of the most prized cuts.
In the United States ribeye is a staple of backyard barbecues and steakhouses.
Butchers often separate lean and fattier sections of ribeye to offer different fat‑content options.
Typical steak thickness is 2–3 cm to allow even cooking.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: Heme iron from beef is highly bioavailable, and zinc supports immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ribeye supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are vital for energy metabolism.

items.title: Creatine source
items.content: Meat contains creatine, which can help improve strength and endurance.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The marbled fat includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly when eaten in moderation.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake of fatty cuts may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor pathogens such as E. coli and salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef proteins.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Large portions can increase uric acid, which is a concern for gout sufferers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ribeye is best enjoyed medium‑rare to retain its juiciness. Season with olive oil, salt, pepper, and herbs, then grill or sear. It pairs well with grilled vegetables, salads, or can be sliced thin for sandwiches. Raw cuts are used for steak tartare but require strict hygiene.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh ribeye in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or a sealed bag, for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed package; quality is maintained for 6‑12 months. Thaw in the fridge, never at room temperature.
